interviewQuestions.question: How would you compute the vertical order traversal of a binary tree, including correct handling of ties?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I assign every node a (row, column) coordinate in a single pass: the root gets column 0, row 0; a left move decreases column by 1 and increases row by 1, a right move increases column by 1 and increases row by 1. I do this with BFS specifically, not DFS — the discovery order matters for the tie-breaking rule.

I group nodes by column into buckets, storing (row, value) pairs as I discover them. Once the traversal is done, I output columns left to right (sorted by column index), and within each column, sort by row — but for nodes that land on the exact same (row, column), the tie-break is 'whichever was discovered first,' which is exactly what BFS's left-to-right, level-by-level discovery order gives for free, since a stable sort by row alone preserves that original BFS order among ties.

The reason BFS matters here and DFS would be risky: DFS commits to one full branch before backtracking to siblings, so it has no guaranteed relationship between visitation order and actual (row, column) position across different branches — a same-column tie could get resolved in the wrong order if the traversal happened to explore a different branch first. BFS's level-by-level guarantee sidesteps that entirely.

Overall this is O(n log n) for the final sort, O(n) for the coordinate-assignment pass.

**Testing:** whether you get the coordinate scheme right and specifically justify why BFS is the safer traversal choice for tie-breaking.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between top view and bottom view of a tree, and how does your implementation change between them?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Both views use the exact same (row, column) coordinate assignment and the same underlying BFS pass — the only thing that changes is which node a column keeps when there's competition. Top view keeps, per column, the node with the smallest row (the shallowest, closest to the root); bottom view keeps the node with the largest row (the deepest).

Implementation-wise, this is genuinely a one-line change if I scan in BFS order and use a simple overwrite rule: for top view, I only write a column's value the first time I see that column (first write wins, since BFS discovers shallower rows before deeper ones); for bottom view, I overwrite every time I see that column again (last write wins, since later BFS discoveries are, by construction, at equal-or-greater depth). Neither needs an explicit row comparison if I trust BFS's discovery order to already be depth-ordered — which it is, level by level.

A subtlety worth naming: this 'first/last write wins' shortcut specifically relies on BFS's guarantee that shallower nodes are always discovered no later than deeper ones. If I were using DFS instead, I'd need to track and explicitly compare row values rather than relying on visitation order, since DFS doesn't provide that depth-ordering guarantee across different branches.

**Testing:** whether you see these as one shared algorithm with a flipped comparison, rather than two unrelated problems to memorize separately.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: View problems

interviewQuestions.question: Why do so many of these 'tree view' problems — vertical order, top/bottom view, diagonal traversal — reduce to the same underlying technique?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because all of them are really asking 'group nodes by some derived coordinate, then apply a per-group rule,' and the only thing that changes between them is which coordinate and which rule.

Vertical order and top/bottom view use (row, column), where column changes on both left and right moves. Diagonal traversal uses a coordinate that only changes on left moves — a right move keeps the same diagonal value as the parent. Right/left view can be framed the same way, as 'group by row, keep last/first per group,' even though it's usually solved more directly with a level-size-snapshot BFS.

Once I recognize a new problem as an instance of this family, solving it becomes two small decisions rather than inventing a new algorithm: what coordinate to assign (and how it changes on left vs. right moves), and what rule picks a winner within a group when there's a tie (first discovered, last discovered, smallest row, largest row). That's a much smaller design space than treating each of these as an unrelated tree problem, and it's also why a BFS-based, coordinate-assignment approach tends to generalize better than trying to special-case each view with a bespoke DFS.

The practical payoff: I can approach an unfamiliar 'view'-style question by asking 'what coordinate would make this a grouping problem' rather than starting from scratch.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate the shared structure behind a family of problems, which is a stronger signal than solving each one correctly in isolation.
